extracted.intended_audience: academic researchers and policymakers studying patent systems and the political economy of regulation
extracted.subtask_description: Historical, cross‑national measurement of patent‑system design: quantitative indicators of discretion granted to patentees, patent offices, and governments (renewal fees, procedural options, extensions, examination/opposition regimes) and covariates describing economic/information environments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Renewal fee ratio (patentee cost skew)
rubrics_metrics.description: The ratio of the costs incurred in the second half of the patent award carried to full term (not including any discretionary extensions) to the total cost in the first half (expressed in nominal dollars). Calculated for 25‑year intervals for a cross‑section of countries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as a measure of discretion/granularity offered to patentees via renewal fee schedules (steepness of schedule). Example effect sizes reported: one standard deviation increase in national population → fee ratio up 51%; one standard deviation increase in exports+imports/GDP → fee ratio up 29%. Table footnotes denote number of renewal fees; assumptions on award timing vary by period (1950+ awards assumed 2 years after application, 1900/1925 assumed 1 year, 1850/1875 assumed nominal).

rubrics_metrics.name: Number of renewal fees
rubrics_metrics.description: Count of renewal payments (footnoted in tables): coded as one (*), two (**), three to five (***), six or more (****).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reported alongside the renewal fee ratio; used to interpret magnitude and frequency of renewal schedule enforcement across periods and countries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentee ability to delay examination (maximum delay years)
rubrics_metrics.description: Maximum length of time (in years from the application date) that a patentee can delay the examination of a patent application (table reports values or 0 if none).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpreted as a patentee discretion mechanism allowing filing of many low‑cost applications that can be activated later (post‑patent learning). Many nations have zero; statistical models use Tobit because many observations are zero (censoring). Table footnotes annotate other procedural features present in that jurisdiction (A,P,U codes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Availability of patents of addition (A)
rubrics_metrics.description: Indicator that patents of addition (improvement patents) can be awarded in the jurisdiction (coded 'A' in procedural tables).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Part of the menu of alternative patent structures that give patentees flexibility; presence is reported by period and country in tables and is used to create counts of alternative schemes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Availability of preliminary patents (P)
rubrics_metrics.description: Indicator that preliminary patent applications (or provisional/preliminary patents) can be awarded (coded 'P').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as one component of the alternative patent structures measure; noted in table annotations and influences patentee discretion patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Availability of utility models / minor patents (U)
rubrics_metrics.description: Indicator that utility models (minor patents, second‑tier protection) are available (coded 'U').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Included in the alternative patent structures count; presence associated with poorer countries in some regressions and used to indicate a menu of lower‑cost/shorter‑term protections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Count of alternative patent structures
rubrics_metrics.description: Count (or ordered measure) of alternative patent forms offered in a country (patents of addition, preliminary patents, utility models).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operationalized with an ordered logit specification to explain cross‑national variation. The paper notes alternative schemes were more frequent in poorer countries and less trade‑intensive ones (in some regressions) and that wealthy nations abandoned some forms (e.g., patents of addition).

rubrics_metrics.name: Discretion of patent office officials to extend awards (maximum extension period)
rubrics_metrics.description: Maximum period that government/patent office officials can extend a domestic patent award without legislative action (reported as years or 'Indef.' for no legislative limit).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treated with a censored regression (extensions cannot be less than zero; some laws left maximum ambiguous). 'Indef.' indicates no legislative limit. This variable captures government discretion to prolong patent terms and is analyzed against economy complexity covariates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Government discretion: selective examination of applications (E)
rubrics_metrics.description: Indicator that government has discretion over which patent applications to examine (coded 'E' in Table 3 notes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listed among other governmental discretionary powers; presence implies administrative filtering power and is used to characterize government control over patent grants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Government discretion to vary fees (F)
rubrics_metrics.description: Indicator that government can vary the fee charged to the patentee (coded 'F').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Part of the set of controls government officials can exert over the patent system; appears as a footnote code and used to interpret cross‑national procedural variation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Government power to license or revoke patents (L and Ls)
rubrics_metrics.description: Indicator that government has the power to license or revoke patents for reasons other than non‑working (L); 'Ls' indicates power to license/revoke some patents (typically pharmaceuticals).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to capture strong governmental interventions (compulsory licensing/revocation) distinct from routine non‑working grounds; reported in Table 3 notes and discussed as a major form of government discretion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Government power to determine original inventor (P, Table 3 meaning)
rubrics_metrics.description: Indicator that the government can determine the original inventor rather than being constrained to award a patent to the first applicant (coded 'P' in Table 3 notes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinct from 'P' in procedural codes for preliminary patents; in Table 3 it denotes a substantive governmental power to resolve inventorship disputes and control award allocation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Government discretion over designated working period (W)
rubrics_metrics.description: Indicator that government has discretion over the working period that is designated for a patent (coded 'W').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listed among government powers in Table 3 notes; relates to post‑grant obligations and potential regulatory control over exploitation of patented inventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Categorical role of patent office in determining novelty (0/1/2)
rubrics_metrics.description: A qualitative dependent variable coded 0 if the patent office had no role in determining novelty, 1 if it had some role, and 2 if it provided full novelty examinations for all patent applications. The middle category includes offices that examine some but not all applications or that only review oppositions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also analyzed alternatively with a dummy for whether the office examined all applications. Results show larger/wealthier nations and those with higher literacy more likely to have full patent‑office novelty examinations (consistent with separating bureaucratic control when monitoring is difficult). Footnote: countries publishing applications prior to issue but with no formal opposition/examination were sometimes included in the middle category with little effect on results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre‑grant opposition and publication regimes (opposition/publishing indicators)
rubrics_metrics.description: Indicators for whether outside parties can oppose patent grants prior to issue and whether applications are published prior to grant (table annotation codes such as Op, OpInt, OpPub, ExS, ExSb etc).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to characterize the nature of the patent examination/opposition regime (e.g., offices that examine and have pre‑grant opposition, offices that do not examine but allow opposition, publication prior to grant). These procedural variants are coded in the tables and influence the coding of the novelty‑examination variable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic/information environment covariates (population, trade intensity, per capita GDP, agricultural employment share, literacy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Country characteristics used as explanatory covariates: national population, ratio of exports+imports to GDP (trade intensity), per‑capita GDP, share of civilian employment in agriculture, literacy rate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These covariates are used to test hypotheses about when discretion is granted and to explain cross‑national variation in patentee and official discretion; findings include that more complex economies (larger population, more trade, lower agricultural share, higher literacy) tend to grant patentees greater procedural discretion (e.g., delayed examinations, steep renewal schedules) while reducing officials' discretionary powers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentee vs. official discretion composite indicators
rubrics_metrics.description: Composite conceptual dimensions comparing discretion granted to patentees (renewal fees, delayed examination, alternative patent forms) versus discretion granted to patent office/government officials (extension rights, licensing/revocation, selective examination, fee variation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Paper analyzes these opposing axes empirically: richer/complex economies tend to shift discretion from officials to patentees (steep renewal schedules, ability to delay examination) while constraining office officials' discretionary powers and increasingly dividing validity determination between offices and courts.
